meta.title: Who really said "Yesterday, December 7, 1941 — a date which will live in infamy — the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: FDR said it to Congress on Dec. 8, 1941. His draft read “world history”; “a day that will live in infamy” is a common misquote.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: The opening sentence of Roosevelt’s address to a joint session of Congress asking for a declaration of war on Japan, delivered December 8, 1941. It is confirmed word for word in the National Archives transcript ↗.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Address to Congress Requesting a Declaration of War with Japan (the “Day of Infamy” speech)
December 8, 1941, to a joint session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C.
“Day of Infamy” Speech, SEN 77A-H1, Record Group 46 (Records of the U.S. Senate), National Archives

source.excerpt: Mr. Vice President, and Mr. Speaker, and Members of the Senate and House of Representatives: Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.
trail: The National Archives ↗ transcribes the speech, starting with this exact sentence. It notes that the first line originally read “a date which will live in world history.”
The American Presidency Project ↗ gives the same opening, dated December 8, 1941.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the sentence in its sourced quotes for Roosevelt, under the address to Congress after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
The National Park Service ↗ also reproduces the address, broadcast from the Capitol on December 8, 1941, at 12:30 p.m.
source.excerptNote: Opening of the speech as given in the National Archives transcript. Some transcriptions, such as Wikisource’s, print the date as “December 7th.”

sourceLink.text: National Archives: Joint Address to Congress Leading to a Declaration of War Against Japan (1941)

source.rightsNote: Roosevelt gave this address as President, so it is a work of the United States Government. Under 17 U.S.C. § 105 ↗, such works get no U.S. copyright protection, even though the speech dates from 1941.

author.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
author.heading: Franklin D. Roosevelt
author.bio: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was the 32nd president of the United States, serving from 1933 until his death in 1945, and the only president elected four times. He led the country through the Great Depression and most of the Second World War. His address to Congress after the attack on Pearl Harbor is one of the best-known speeches in American history.

misattribution.heading: The common mix-ups
misattribution.intro: Nobody doubts that Roosevelt said this. The errors are in the wording: the famous phrase is often misquoted, and his draft used a different word.

items.who: “A day that will live in infamy”
items.why: This is the way most people repeat the line, but Roosevelt said “a date which will live in infamy.” Wikipedia ↗ notes the misquote and points out that Roosevelt stressed the date, December 7, 1941.

items.who: “A date which will live in world history”
items.why: This is how the first line read in the draft, before Roosevelt revised it. The National Archives ↗ calls that revision the most significant change he made to the speech. The draft wording was never delivered.

misattribution.truthLine: What Roosevelt said on December 8, 1941: “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan” (National Archives transcript ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Roosevelt spoke to a joint session of Congress on December 8, 1941, the day after the attack on Pearl Harbor. The speech was also broadcast to the nation by radio. It ended with a request that Congress declare that a state of war existed with Japan.
Roosevelt revised the opening line, replacing “world history” with “infamy.” The National Archives ↗ calls this the most significant change he made to the speech.
context.pull: “…a date which will live in infamy…”
